notes.claim: During charging, electrolysis decomposes the water of the electrolyte into hydrogen and oxygen.
Hydrogen and oxygen are produced more quickly near full charge, and continued charging after full charge produces a lot of gas.
Above the gassing voltage of 2.40 V per cell, one maker recommends limiting the charging current to 2.5 to 5 A per 100 Ah.
HSE gives the natural-ventilation opening area as 0.3 x N x I x S cm2, with N cells, I the overcharging current in amps, and S the dilution factor.
HSE says to use the maximum current the charger is likely to supply during a malfunction, to include a suitable safety margin.
HSE design limits for hydrogen are 0.4 per cent in areas people enter and 1 per cent in enclosures people do not enter.
Hydrogen in air ignites and explodes readily between 4 per cent (lower limit) and 75 per cent (upper limit).
Battery-room ventilation air should be exhausted to the outside and never recirculated into other confined areas.
Where mechanical ventilation is used, an alarm should detect a hydrogen build-up or a failed fan.
HSE's opening rule assumes air crosses each ventilation opening at 0.1 m/s or more.
Another safety body gives hydrogen's flammable range in air as 4.1 to 72 per cent, a little different from HSE's 4 to 75 per cent.
Leave a battery to stand for at least 20 minutes after charging so flammable gas can disperse.

sources.title: Using electric storage batteries safely INDG139 — HSE
sources.quote: In charging areas that people enter (workrooms) the concentration of hydrogen should not exceed 0.4% vol/vol (10% of the LEL).

sources.title: Using electric storage batteries safely INDG139 — HSE
sources.quote: When charging takes place in an enclosure that people do not enter, the concentration of hydrogen should not exceed 1% vol/vol (25% of the LEL).
